one_sentence: The Beer-Lambert law of exponential absorption maps identically to transaction fee extraction, showing that mandatory digital payment infrastructure imposes a structural, physics-like decay on purchasing power.
executive_summary: This document establishes a structural isomorphism between the Beer-Lambert law in optics and transaction fee extraction in economics. In optics, light intensity decays exponentially through an absorptive medium, with the absorption coefficient set by the medium, not the signal. In economics, purchasing power decays exponentially through a fee-extracting payment infrastructure, with the fee rate set by intermediaries, not the transacting parties. The mathematical forms are identical: I(x) = I₀·e^(-αx) maps to P(n) = P₀·(1-f)^n ≈ P₀·e^(-fn). The key insight is that the extraction rate is a property of the medium, not the signal—buyers cannot choose the interchange fee, just as photons cannot choose their absorption. The document tests this mapping bidirectionally, passes the swap test, and makes falsifiable predictions: as cash is eliminated and digital payment becomes mandatory, intermediary revenue as a share of GDP should increase, and high-frequency, low-value transactors (disproportionately the poor) will be most affected. The theological layer invokes Proverbs 11:1 on false balances and the Cantillon effect, framing the shift from cash (lossless) to mandatory digital payment (lossy) as a coherence-degrading structural change.
short_summary: This document is a structural isomorphism record mapping the Beer-Lambert law of exponential absorption to transaction fee extraction in digital payment systems. The core claim is that purchasing power decays exponentially through fee-extracting infrastructure, with the fee rate set by the medium (intermediaries) rather than the signal (transactors). Key evidence includes the identical mathematical form (I = I₀·e^(-αx) vs. P = P₀·(1-f)^n), the swap test passing bidirectionally, and falsifiable predictions about intermediary GDP share and disproportionate impact on the poor. This matters because it reveals that mandatory digital payment infrastructure imposes a physics-like, passive extraction on economic activity, with moral and structural implications for economic justice and coherence.
